chapterTitle: Multi-Account Security Strategy and AWS Organizations
aiGenerationNote: Create a 12-minute animated video explaining multi-account strategies. Start with a visual analogy of a large company with different departments (accounts) and centralized HR/Security (Organizations). Show the hierarchical structure of OUs and how SCPs (represented as security gates or rules) are applied. Include a split-screen demo showing an SCP being created and attached in the AWS console, followed by an attempt to perform a denied action in a member account, illustrating the "Access Denied" error. Emphasize the difference between SCPs and IAM policies. End with a reflection prompt asking learners to consider their current organization's structure and how it could benefit from OUs and SCPs.

screens.title: Multi-Account Security Strategy and AWS Organizations
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll treat a multi-account strategy as a foundational security primitive. You will learn why moving from a monolithic single-account model to a structured, multi-account architecture reduces blast radius, simplifies compliance, and centralizes governance. We'll introduce AWS Organizations as the central control plane, explain how Organizational Units let you group accounts for consistent policy application, and show how Service Control Policies act as guardrails that limit what member accounts can ever do. I'll give concrete examples such as preventing production accounts from creating resources in unapproved regions and an SCP that blocks stopping CloudTrail. We'll also cover planning patterns: a security tooling account for centralized logging, environment-based OUs for dev and prod separation, and the inheritance behavior that can cause unexpected denials if an SCP is applied too broadly. By the end you'll understand what decisions create operational friction and what choices reduce risk, plus a short exercise to create a restrictive SCP and test it safely in a sandbox account. Think of this lesson as the playbook you can use to plan account boundaries that match compliance, operations, and security objectives.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives will guide what you practice and measure. First, you will design a multi-account strategy that separates security, operations, and billing responsibilities. That means deciding which accounts become production, which hold shared infrastructure, and where security tools collect logs. A concrete example is placing Transit Gateway in an Infrastructure OU so network services are centrally managed, while applications live in environment OUs. Second, you will implement Service Control Policies to enforce guardrails across accounts. SCPs are not grants; they only restrict. A practical task is creating an SCP that prevents stopping CloudTrail. Third, you will structure Organizational Units so they match compliance boundaries and operational models. Use a Security OU for logging and a Production OU for stricter rules. Finally, you will identify and mitigate common risks like overbroad denies or missing security tooling accounts. For each objective you will see a simple mnemonic or milestone to verify competency and a suggested scenario to test safely in a sandbox account. Keep these objectives in mind as you progress; they map directly to real operational tasks you will perform when governing an enterprise AWS environment.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Verification
screens.narratorSegment: This companion objectives slide turns each learning objective into a verification activity you can run. For account design, verify billing separation and that production workloads cannot access development resources unless explicitly shared. An example verification is checking consolidated billing shows separate cost centers per account. For SCPs, create a deny SCP that blocks stopping CloudTrail and attach it to a non-production OU first; then attempt the action in a sandbox member account and observe an explicit denial. For OUs, confirm inheritance by applying a read-only guardrail at a parent OU and seeing it affect nested accounts. For mitigation, run a policy review to find SCP statements with broad resource wildcards or actions that apply to all regions, and then refine conditions or move the SCP to a narrower OU. Each of these verification steps ensures the theoretical design translates into observable controls. The goal is that when you hand off accounts to teams, you can show measurable evidence that guardrails are functioning.

screens.title: Why a multi-account strategy matters
screens.narratorSegment: A multi-account strategy separates responsibilities and limits impact when incidents happen. In a single-account model, a compromised credential or misconfiguration can affect every workload and every environment. By contrast, splitting workloads across accounts confines failures to a smaller scope and simplifies incident response. For example, if a dataset in a development account is exposed, that breach does not necessarily lead to production outages or billing surprises. Multi-account design also enables clearer ownership: teams can manage their own account-level IAM policies while central governance applies organization-wide rules like mandatory logging. This separation supports compliance too—regulatory controls that require data segmentation or strict auditing are easier to meet when accounts mirror those boundaries. A common misconception is that more accounts automatically increase complexity without benefit. The correct lens is to design purposeful accounts aligned to operational boundaries and to adopt automation for provisioning and baseline configuration. The practical takeaway is to view account boundaries as low-cost, high-value controls that complement IAM and network isolation, and to ensure each account starts with baseline guardrails and a centralized security shipping point for logs and alerts. How would you map your critical applications into accounts to minimize blast radius?

keyIdea.text: Multi-account design reduces blast radius and creates manageable ownership, billing separation, and compliance boundaries.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Why multi-account
Definition and purpose

A multi-account strategy divides workloads and responsibilities across accounts to contain risk and simplify governance.

Isolation
Limits the blast radius of security incidents or failures.
Governance
Centralized rules can be applied while teams retain account-level control.
Billing & Ownership
Clear cost centers and ownership for auditing and chargeback.
Concrete example
Production account: holds live services and strict SCPs Development account: sandbox for engineers Security account: collects CloudTrail and GuardDuty findings
Common misconception

Some teams fear too many accounts add overhead. The real risk is poorly planned accounts. Use automation and templates for baselines so additional accounts do not increase operational cost significantly.

Key Takeaway

Design accounts to map to operational or compliance boundaries; automate baselines to avoid manual drift.

screens.title: AWS Organizations as the control plane
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Organizations provides a central control plane to create and manage accounts, group them into Organizational Units, and attach Service Control Policies. Think of Organizations as the governance layer that can enforce broad guardrails while member accounts retain local IAM choices. A useful analogy is centralized HR applying company policies while individual departments manage day-to-day tasks. Organizations supports a hierarchical OU model: OUs can be nested to reflect structure such as Security → Infrastructure → Applications. Policies attached to a parent OU are inherited by children, so a deny applied at the root affects every descendant account. This inheritance is powerful but can surprise teams if an overly broad deny is placed high in the tree. For example, denying s3:DeleteBucket at the root will prevent deletion in development and production unless the SCP is narrowed. Practically, you will create a Management Account to pay bills and manage membership, a Security account for tools and logs, and member accounts for workloads. Always plan where to attach SCPs and test them in sandbox OUs. What organizational hierarchy in your environment will make policy application predictable and safe?

keyIdea.title: Organizations role
keyIdea.text: AWS Organizations centralizes account lifecycle, OU grouping, and the attachment of SCP guardrails that are inherited by child OUs and accounts.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › AWS Organizations
Control plane responsibilities
  • Manage account creation and organization membership.
  • Group accounts into OUs for policy application and inheritance.
  • Attach Service Control Policies to define maximum permissions.
Remember: Organizations does not grant permissions; it constrains them via SCPs applied at organizational boundaries.
Architecture snapshot
Management Account
Pays bills and manages organization membership and SCP lifecycle.
Security OU / Account
Central logging, CloudTrail, and monitoring services are collected here.
Environment OUs
Dev, Test, Prod OUs allow environment-specific guardrails and workflows.
Misconception

Organizations alone do not enforce resource-level access; SCPs restrict actions but IAM still grants explicit permissions within those bounds.

screens.title: Designing OU structure
screens.narratorSegment: Organizational Units let you apply policies to groups of accounts and do so hierarchically. A common pattern is to create OUs for Security, Infrastructure, and environment types like Development, Test, and Production. The Security OU hosts logging and detection tools so that logs and alerts are centralized. Infrastructure OUs contain shared networking or identity resources. The OU hierarchy should be deep enough to target policies precisely but not so complex that you lose visibility. For instance, adding an OU per microservice team may become unmanageable; instead, prefer OUs that represent administrative or compliance boundaries. Important to remember: SCPs applied at a parent OU are inherited by children. That means a deny at the root affects all accounts, which can be desirable for safety but can also break legitimate operations if not planned. When designing OUs, document which SCPs attach where, create a sandbox OU for testing, and automate account provisioning so every new account receives the correct baseline SCPs. A practical test is to attach a read-only SCP to a parent OU and confirm a nested account cannot perform writes that otherwise its IAM would allow. Would your organization benefit from environment-based OUs, or are business-unit OUs a better fit?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › OU design
Hierarchy patterns
  1. 1. Security OU for logging and central detection tools.
  2. 2. Infrastructure OU for shared networking and directory services.
  3. 3. Environment OUs for Dev, Test, and Prod separation.
Keep OU structure predictable and documented so team onboarding and policy audits are straightforward.
Practical checklist
Automation
Provision accounts with a baseline template and attach required SCPs automatically.
Sandbox OU
Test new SCPs in an isolated OU before wide attachment.
Document attachments
Record which SCPs are attached to each OU and why to avoid surprises.
Common mistake

Applying an overly broad SCP at a high-level OU can unintentionally deny needed actions in many accounts. Prefer narrow attachments when possible.

screens.title: What SCPs are and how they work
screens.narratorSegment: Service Control Policies set the upper bound of what an account can do. They are JSON documents attached to OUs or accounts that evaluate before IAM policies. Because SCPs only restrict, they cannot be used to give a permission that IAM does not already allow. For example, an SCP that denies the action to stop CloudTrail ensures that even an administrator in a member account cannot disable logging. A concrete misunderstanding is to treat SCPs like IAM allow lists; instead, view them as organization-enforced cannot-do lists. Use SCPs to enforce requirements such as mandatory MFA for root, region restrictions for resource creation, or preventing accounts from leaving the organization. When writing SCPs, test them in a sandbox OU and include specific conditions to avoid blocking normal operations. Also remember SCPs inherit down the OU hierarchy: an SCP on a parent OU affects every child. A good practice is to attach global denies only where absolutely necessary and to use narrower SCPs for environment-specific rules. When you design your first SCP, name it clearly and include a comment in your repository that explains the intended coverage and test plan.

keyIdea.title: SCP behavior
keyIdea.text: SCPs restrict available permissions across accounts; they do not grant permissions and are evaluated before IAM.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › SCP fundamentals
SCP definition

An SCP is a JSON policy attached to an OU or account that denies or allows actions in member accounts but does not grant permissions by itself.

Key property
SCPs limit the maximum available permissions; IAM still controls effective permissions within that bound.
When to use
Use SCPs for organization-wide guardrails like preventing account removal or disabling logging.
Concrete example
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": [
        "organizations:LeaveOrganization",
        "cloudtrail:StopLogging",
        "cloudtrail:DeleteTrail"
      ],
      "Resource": "*"
    }
  ]
}
This SCP prevents member accounts from leaving the organization or stopping CloudTrail, enforcing continuity of logs.
Misconception

An SCP is not a substitute for fine-grained IAM policies; use both together for defense in depth.

screens.title: SCPs versus IAM policies
screens.narratorSegment: It is essential to distinguish Service Control Policies and IAM policies. SCPs are attached at the organization or OU level and define the maximum an account can do. IAM policies are attached to users, groups, and roles inside an account and grant specific permissions. A useful way to think about this: SCPs answer the question 'what actions are never allowed across these accounts?', while IAM answers 'what actions is this principal explicitly allowed to perform?'. For example, if an SCP denies s3:DeleteBucket, then no IAM policy in a member account can enable bucket deletion, even if an administrator writes an allow. A common misconception is that an allow in an SCP will grant permissions; SCP allows only remove restrictions and cannot elevate privileges. Practically, use SCPs for blunt, organization-wide constraints — stop actions that violate policy — and use IAM for fine-grained role-based access. When auditing, check both planes: a permissive IAM policy under an overbroad SCP can be silently ineffective, and a missing IAM allow under a narrow SCP will still prevent operations. The closing question: are your current IAM policies redundant under your SCPs, and can you simplify them?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › SCP vs IAM
Service Control Policies
  • Applied at OU or account level
  • Define maximum available actions
  • Inherited by child OUs
Example: Deny stopping CloudTrail everywhere by attaching an SCP to the Production OU.
IAM Policies
  • Attached to principals inside accounts
  • Grant permissions within the SCP bounds
  • Used for fine-grained role access
Example: Grant a role permission to manage EC2 instances only in approved regions, while SCP restricts regions organization-wide.
Key Takeaway

Use SCPs for broad guardrails and IAM for precise access. Audit both to ensure intended behavior.

screens.title: Preventing account removal and disabling CloudTrail
screens.narratorSegment: Here is a practical SCP you can use as a template to prevent member accounts from leaving the organization and from disabling CloudTrail. This policy has a Deny effect on three actions: leaving the organization, stopping CloudTrail logging, and deleting trails. Because the Resource is a wildcard, the deny covers all relevant resources in attached accounts. Place a policy like this on OUs that must never be able to remove logging or remove membership, typically a Production OU or a Security OU. Before attaching widely, test in a sandbox OU and attempt the denied actions to confirm the explicit denial messages. Also be careful with management account permissions: the management account can change organizational attachments, so protect that root contact and use MFA. Remember that while SCPs prevent actions, audit trails remain the key to proving that a denial occurred and why. After you paste this JSON into the policy editor, attach it to a test OU and verify that a non-privileged admin in a member account cannot stop CloudTrail. That verification is the best evidence your guardrail works. Preventing account removal and disabling CloudTrail means a deny scp blocks organizations:leaveorganization and cloudtrail stop or delete actions to protect logging and membership.. In practical terms, an scp example that denies leaving the organization and stopping logs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › SCP example
SCP JSON
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": [
        "organizations:LeaveOrganization",
        "cloudtrail:StopLogging",
        "cloudtrail:DeleteTrail"
      ],
      "Resource": "*"
    }
  ]

Attach this SCP to an OU to ensure member accounts cannot disable logging or remove themselves from the organization.
Example test
Attach to sandbox OU, then in a member account try to stop CloudTrail and observe an explicit Access Denied message.
Pro tip
Protect the management account with strict controls and MFA, since it manages policy attachments and billing.

screens.title: Enforce allowed regions and S3 bucket deletion guardrail
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on SCP enforces two practical restrictions: it denies launching EC2 instances in any region other than approved ones and it prevents deletion of S3 buckets that contain 'prod-data' in the bucket name. The first statement uses a condition on the requested region to deny RunInstances when the region does not equal allowed values. The second statement explicitly denies s3:DeleteBucket for ARNs that match a pattern. This demonstrates how SCPs can express both action restrictions and resource-based constraints. Important to note: when you use wildcard ARNs with SCPs, test carefully because overly broad patterns can block unrelated buckets. The recommended workflow is to create the policy in the management account, attach it to a Production OU test account, then attempt an EC2 launch in an unapproved region and a deletion of a bucket named my-prod-data-backup. You should receive explicit denials. Always refine conditions or resource patterns based on test results so you avoid disrupting normal operations in development. This activity helps you combine region controls and resource name patterns into enforceable organizational guardrails. Enforce allowed regions and S3 bucket deletion guardrail means use conditions and resource patterns in scps to restrict regions and prevent deletion of critical production buckets.. In practical terms, an scp example that denies launching ec2 outside approved regions and prevents deleting prod-data buckets. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Hands-on SCP
Policy JSON (template)
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": "ec2:RunInstances",
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "StringNotEquals": {
          "aws:RequestedRegion": [
            "us-east-1",
            "eu-west-1"
          ]
        }
      }
    },
    {
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": "s3:DeleteBucket",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::*prod-data*",
      "Condition": {
        "StringLike": { "s3:prefix": ["*"] }
      }
    }
  ]
}
Attach to your Production OU. Then try launching EC2 in Sydney or deleting a bucket named my-prod-data-backup to confirm denials.
Test steps
  1. Create SCP in Management Account.
  2. Attach to sandbox Production OU.
  3. Attempt denied actions in member account.
Caution
Wildcard ARNs can block more than intended. Test broadly named patterns in a sandbox first.

screens.title: Planning account provisioning and migration
screens.narratorSegment: A planned provisioning and migration workflow reduces surprises when bringing workloads into a multi-account organization. Start by defining account templates that include baseline IAM roles, enforced SCPs, logging configuration, and required tags for billing. Next, create an automated provisioning pipeline to instantiate accounts with those templates and attach them to the correct OU. When migrating an existing workload, first replicate the required baseline in a sandbox member account and attach the same SCPs you plan to use in production. Then perform a staged migration, verifying logging, networking connectivity, and IAM role mappings at each step. An essential step is to test SCPs early; a misconfigured SCP can block critical operations and delay migration. Also include rollback plans so you can detach or adjust SCPs if an unexpected denial prevents required operations. A common mistake is to migrate quickly without applying SCPs until after cutover; that leaves a gap where production controls are not yet enforced. The practical takeaway is to treat account creation and migration as automated, auditable steps that include testing and rollback, not one-off manual tasks. screens.title: Common mistakes and how to avoid them
screens.narratorSegment: Many multi-account implementations stumble on a few recurring problems. One mistake is using a flat account structure without OUs; that forces per-account policy management and negates the benefits of centralized governance. Another is attaching overbroad SCPs at the root, which can unintentionally stop legitimate operations across the organization. A third is failing to create a dedicated security tooling account early, scattering logs and making incident response harder. To avoid these, adopt clear OU boundaries, attach narrowly scoped SCPs, and set up a Security OU for CloudTrail and detection services. When writing SCPs, prefer deny statements with specific actions and resource patterns, and include conditions to narrow the scope. Also create a sandbox OU to validate new policies and add automated tests that simulate common admin tasks to detect unintended denials. Finally, document intended SCP effects and include rollback steps. Addressing these mistakes early in design prevents costly operational disruption later. content.html:

Flat structure
No OUs means policy scaling problems and manual configuration drift.
Overbroad SCPs
Root-level denies can accidentally block needed actions. Narrow where possible.
Missing security account
Without a centralized security account, logs and alerts are fragmented and response slows.
Practical steps

screens.title: Baseline security and observability accounts
screens.narratorSegment: A dedicated security tooling account is a common and effective best practice. It centralizes CloudTrail logs, GuardDuty findings, Security Hub, and any long-term archives. Centralization simplifies alerts and makes incident response faster because investigators have a single place to query historical activity. When designing the security account, ensure CloudTrail streams from all member accounts into a centralized S3 bucket with lifecycle and immutability policies. Also forward findings from threat detection services to the security account's aggregator so analysts can correlate events across accounts. The management account should remain limited to organization-level operations and billing; protect it with strict access controls and multi-factor authentication. One misconception is that centralization creates a single point of failure — centralization for observability is about visibility, not centralized control. Keep actual service operations distributed in their respective accounts while using the security account as the telemetry hub. The practical question is: do you have a plan for central log ingestion, retention, and secure access that scales as you add accounts? Baseline security and observability accounts means centralize logs and detection in a security account to accelerate incident response and maintain consistent audit trails across accounts.. screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.narratorSegment: These are the core concepts you should carry forward. First, AWS Organizations is the central service to manage accounts, OUs, and policy attachments. It gives you a single control plane for governance. Second, an Organizational Unit groups AWS accounts so you can attach policies to multiple accounts at once and rely on predictable inheritance. Third, a Service Control Policy is an organization-level JSON policy that defines maximum permissions; SCPs deny actions even when local IAM policies attempt to allow them. Each concept plays a distinct role: Organizations provides structure, OUs provide grouping and inheritance, and SCPs provide enforced guardrails. Hold these definitions in mind as vocabulary you will use when designing account boundaries and drafting policies. A practical reminder: when you write an SCP, test it in a sandbox OU before attaching it broadly so you avoid unintended denials.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 2
screens.narratorSegment: Finish by remembering three operational terms you will use daily. The Root Account is the primary account for an organization and should be tightly secured because it has ultimate control. The Management Account is the payer and the administrative control point for Organizations; protect it and restrict who can change organization-wide attachments. A Member Account is any account under the management account; those host workloads and receive inherited SCPs. Finally, blast radius is the concept describing the potential scope of damage from an incident. Multi-account strategies reduce blast radius by isolating services and data into separate accounts. These operational roles pair with governance controls: protect the root and management accounts, centralize logging into the security account, and design OUs and SCPs to shrink the blast radius for any breach. As a reflection, check whether your highest privilege accounts have MFA, and whether your account boundaries would limit harm in a compromise.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll treat a multi-account strategy as a foundational security primitive. You will learn why moving from a monolithic single-account model to a structured, multi-account architecture reduces blast radius, simplifies compliance, and centralizes governance. We'll introduce AWS Organizations as the central control plane, explain how Organizational Units let you group accounts for consistent policy application, and show how Service Control Policies act as guardrails that limit what member accounts can ever do. I'll give concrete examples such as preventing production accounts from creating resources in unapproved regions and an SCP that blocks stopping CloudTrail. We'll also cover planning patterns: a security tooling account for centralized logging, environment-based OUs for dev and prod separation, and the inheritance behavior that can cause unexpected denials if an SCP is applied too broadly. By the end you'll understand what decisions create operational friction and what choices reduce risk, plus a short exercise to create a restrictive SCP and test it safely in a sandbox account. Think of this lesson as the playbook you can use to plan account boundaries that match compliance, operations, and security objectives.

These learning objectives will guide what you practice and measure. First, you will design a multi-account strategy that separates security, operations, and billing responsibilities. That means deciding which accounts become production, which hold shared infrastructure, and where security tools collect logs. A concrete example is placing Transit Gateway in an Infrastructure OU so network services are centrally managed, while applications live in environment OUs. Second, you will implement Service Control Policies to enforce guardrails across accounts. SCPs are not grants; they only restrict. A practical task is creating an SCP that prevents stopping CloudTrail. Third, you will structure Organizational Units so they match compliance boundaries and operational models. Use a Security OU for logging and a Production OU for stricter rules. Finally, you will identify and mitigate common risks like overbroad denies or missing security tooling accounts. For each objective you will see a simple mnemonic or milestone to verify competency and a suggested scenario to test safely in a sandbox account. Keep these objectives in mind as you progress; they map directly to real operational tasks you will perform when governing an enterprise AWS environment.

This companion objectives slide turns each learning objective into a verification activity you can run. For account design, verify billing separation and that production workloads cannot access development resources unless explicitly shared. An example verification is checking consolidated billing shows separate cost centers per account. For SCPs, create a deny SCP that blocks stopping CloudTrail and attach it to a non-production OU first; then attempt the action in a sandbox member account and observe an explicit denial. For OUs, confirm inheritance by applying a read-only guardrail at a parent OU and seeing it affect nested accounts. For mitigation, run a policy review to find SCP statements with broad resource wildcards or actions that apply to all regions, and then refine conditions or move the SCP to a narrower OU. Each of these verification steps ensures the theoretical design translates into observable controls. The goal is that when you hand off accounts to teams, you can show measurable evidence that guardrails are functioning.

A multi-account strategy separates responsibilities and limits impact when incidents happen. In a single-account model, a compromised credential or misconfiguration can affect every workload and every environment. By contrast, splitting workloads across accounts confines failures to a smaller scope and simplifies incident response. For example, if a dataset in a development account is exposed, that breach does not necessarily lead to production outages or billing surprises. Multi-account design also enables clearer ownership: teams can manage their own account-level IAM policies while central governance applies organization-wide rules like mandatory logging. This separation supports compliance too—regulatory controls that require data segmentation or strict auditing are easier to meet when accounts mirror those boundaries. A common misconception is that more accounts automatically increase complexity without benefit. The correct lens is to design purposeful accounts aligned to operational boundaries and to adopt automation for provisioning and baseline configuration. The practical takeaway is to view account boundaries as low-cost, high-value controls that complement IAM and network isolation, and to ensure each account starts with baseline guardrails and a centralized security shipping point for logs and alerts. How would you map your critical applications into accounts to minimize blast radius?

AWS Organizations provides a central control plane to create and manage accounts, group them into Organizational Units, and attach Service Control Policies. Think of Organizations as the governance layer that can enforce broad guardrails while member accounts retain local IAM choices. A useful analogy is centralized HR applying company policies while individual departments manage day-to-day tasks. Organizations supports a hierarchical OU model: OUs can be nested to reflect structure such as Security → Infrastructure → Applications. Policies attached to a parent OU are inherited by children, so a deny applied at the root affects every descendant account. This inheritance is powerful but can surprise teams if an overly broad deny is placed high in the tree. For example, denying s3:DeleteBucket at the root will prevent deletion in development and production unless the SCP is narrowed. Practically, you will create a Management Account to pay bills and manage membership, a Security account for tools and logs, and member accounts for workloads. Always plan where to attach SCPs and test them in sandbox OUs. What organizational hierarchy in your environment will make policy application predictable and safe?

Organizational Units let you apply policies to groups of accounts and do so hierarchically. A common pattern is to create OUs for Security, Infrastructure, and environment types like Development, Test, and Production. The Security OU hosts logging and detection tools so that logs and alerts are centralized. Infrastructure OUs contain shared networking or identity resources. The OU hierarchy should be deep enough to target policies precisely but not so complex that you lose visibility. For instance, adding an OU per microservice team may become unmanageable; instead, prefer OUs that represent administrative or compliance boundaries. Important to remember: SCPs applied at a parent OU are inherited by children. That means a deny at the root affects all accounts, which can be desirable for safety but can also break legitimate operations if not planned. When designing OUs, document which SCPs attach where, create a sandbox OU for testing, and automate account provisioning so every new account receives the correct baseline SCPs. A practical test is to attach a read-only SCP to a parent OU and confirm a nested account cannot perform writes that otherwise its IAM would allow. Would your organization benefit from environment-based OUs, or are business-unit OUs a better fit?

Service Control Policies set the upper bound of what an account can do. They are JSON documents attached to OUs or accounts that evaluate before IAM policies. Because SCPs only restrict, they cannot be used to give a permission that IAM does not already allow. For example, an SCP that denies the action to stop CloudTrail ensures that even an administrator in a member account cannot disable logging. A concrete misunderstanding is to treat SCPs like IAM allow lists; instead, view them as organization-enforced cannot-do lists. Use SCPs to enforce requirements such as mandatory MFA for root, region restrictions for resource creation, or preventing accounts from leaving the organization. When writing SCPs, test them in a sandbox OU and include specific conditions to avoid blocking normal operations. Also remember SCPs inherit down the OU hierarchy: an SCP on a parent OU affects every child. A good practice is to attach global denies only where absolutely necessary and to use narrower SCPs for environment-specific rules. When you design your first SCP, name it clearly and include a comment in your repository that explains the intended coverage and test plan.

It is essential to distinguish Service Control Policies and IAM policies. SCPs are attached at the organization or OU level and define the maximum an account can do. IAM policies are attached to users, groups, and roles inside an account and grant specific permissions. A useful way to think about this: SCPs answer the question 'what actions are never allowed across these accounts?', while IAM answers 'what actions is this principal explicitly allowed to perform?'. For example, if an SCP denies s3:DeleteBucket, then no IAM policy in a member account can enable bucket deletion, even if an administrator writes an allow. A common misconception is that an allow in an SCP will grant permissions; SCP allows only remove restrictions and cannot elevate privileges. Practically, use SCPs for blunt, organization-wide constraints — stop actions that violate policy — and use IAM for fine-grained role-based access. When auditing, check both planes: a permissive IAM policy under an overbroad SCP can be silently ineffective, and a missing IAM allow under a narrow SCP will still prevent operations. The closing question: are your current IAM policies redundant under your SCPs, and can you simplify them?

This policy has a Deny effect on three actions: leaving the organization, stopping CloudTrail logging, and deleting trails. Because the Resource is a wildcard, the deny covers all relevant resources in attached accounts. Also be careful with management account permissions: the management account can change organizational attachments, so protect that root contact and use MFA. Remember that while SCPs prevent actions, audit trails remain the key to proving that a denial occurred and why. After you paste this JSON into the policy editor, attach it to a test OU and verify that a non-privileged admin in a member account cannot stop CloudTrail. These are the core concepts you should carry forward. First, AWS Organizations is the central service to manage accounts, OUs, and policy attachments. It gives you a single control plane for governance. Second, an Organizational Unit groups AWS accounts so you can attach policies to multiple accounts at once and rely on predictable inheritance. Third, a Service Control Policy is an organization-level JSON policy that defines maximum permissions; SCPs deny actions even when local IAM policies attempt to allow them. Each concept plays a distinct role: Organizations provides structure, OUs provide grouping and inheritance, and SCPs provide enforced guardrails. Hold these definitions in mind as vocabulary you will use when designing account boundaries and drafting policies. A practical reminder: when you write an SCP, test it in a sandbox OU before attaching it broadly so you avoid unintended denials.

Finish by remembering three operational terms you will use daily. The Root Account is the primary account for an organization and should be tightly secured because it has ultimate control. The Management Account is the payer and the administrative control point for Organizations; protect it and restrict who can change organization-wide attachments. A Member Account is any account under the management account; those host workloads and receive inherited SCPs. Finally, blast radius is the concept describing the potential scope of damage from an incident. Multi-account strategies reduce blast radius by isolating services and data into separate accounts. These operational roles pair with governance controls: protect the root and management accounts, centralize logging into the security account, and design OUs and SCPs to shrink the blast radius for any breach. As a reflection, check whether your highest privilege accounts have MFA, and whether your account boundaries would limit harm in a compromise.
